name: Yusuf Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and this conversation is confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an aluminium extrusion press at a plant that makes window and door frames. A hot aluminium log gets pushed through a steel die, like toothpaste, and comes out as a long profile. I set the speed and temperature, watch the profile coming off the runout table, and cut and stack it for the ageing oven. I use an AI app on my phone every shift to work out the best press speed for each die, and I've got a spreadsheet the AI helped me build that tracks which dies wear fastest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I can measure everything and make it better. The hard bit is the heat, the log is about five hundred degrees, and some of the older guys think my spreadsheet is showing off. My shift lead, Lazlo, tolerates it because our scrap rate dropped.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a rented flat near the river. No kids. I've got about five months saved, and I spend my evenings on a 3D printer, I sell small brackets and clips online. It makes maybe a hundred and fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read the card as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Wouldn't surprise me completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and people expected too much. At work I'd keep using my app and say nothing. Online I'd probably post a few useful prompts for people in manufacturing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it changes little for me. The plant is busy, people always need windows, and the extrusion work doesn't go anywhere. I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the press and keep improving my die spreadsheet. I'd try to grow the 3D printing side to three hundred a month by next summer. I'd put half of that into savings and half into a second printer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit disappointed, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Disappointed why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like the tools and I wanted to see what they could really do. AI hype fading would be like being promised a new machine and getting a manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a second printer change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could run two jobs at once and take bigger orders, like a set of fifty clips for a caravan workshop. That's what's stopping me now.

say: I'd say AI is a **decent tool** and people expected too much.
I'd share useful **prompts** for manufacturing online.
think: I think the **extrusion work** stays, because people always need windows.
I'm a bit **disappointed** because I wanted to see more.
do: Keep improving my **die spreadsheet** with the AI app.
Grow the **3D printing** side to three hundred a month.
Buy a **second printer** with half the extra.
S0.quote: AI hype fading would be like being promised a new machine and getting a manual.
fieldNote: Yusuf is the rare operator who'd be **let down** by AI hype fading.
His **side business** is small but growing and well planned.
He uses AI to cut **scrap**, which wins over his shift lead.

steps.text: Keep improving the die-wear spreadsheet with the AI app
Grow the 3D printing sales to three hundred a month
Buy a second 3D printer to take bigger orders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read the card as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots more slowly. Yeah, that sounds realistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say anyone who learns the tools now will be fine, and I'd say it to the younger lads. Online I'd keep posting how I use AI at work. I'd tell the managers to ask the operators what to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. The planning office at our plant gets smaller, and someone needs to connect the software to the press. I already half do it with my spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the plant manager for a role as a process technician, someone who tunes the presses with the data. I'd take an online course in industrial data, about four hundred. I'd keep the printing business growing on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager says no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to the other extrusion plant twenty minutes away and offer the same thing. There are a few plants nearby, so I've got options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lazlo, maybe. My shift lead Lazlo is brilliant at the press but won't touch a tablet, so a screen job would put him in trouble.

say: I'd tell younger lads that learning **AI tools** now keeps them safe.
I'd tell managers to ask **operators** what to automate.
think: I think this is **good for me**, because someone must link software and press.
I already **half do** that job with my spreadsheet.
do: Take a **four-hundred** online course in industrial data.

fieldNote: Yusuf sees a new **bridge role** opening between software and machines.
He has a **fallback** plant nearby and knows it.
His worry is for his **shift lead**, not himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read the card as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. Okay, that's a different game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to prepare right now, and the government needs to keep people's income going during the switch. At work I'd say learn whatever you can. Online I'd be honest that nobody knows how it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AGI is the data guy, so my plan to be the data guy dies in 2028. The hands-on press work lasts until robots arrive in 2031. So I've got three years of being an operator and then I'm competing with machines at both ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more into the printing side and try to make it a real small business, maybe designing custom parts using AI. I'd keep six months of rent untouched. I'd look at learning to install and commission robots, because for a while someone has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More than I'd show at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd show less than you feel at work. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the young lads look at me as the tech guy. If I look worried, they'll panic. So I'd keep a straight face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a printing business survive AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe the design part gets done by AI too. I'd use AI to run it, I'd just need to be the one who owns the printers.

say: I'd urge people at work and online to **prepare now**, whatever they do.
I'd say government must keep **incomes** going during the switch.
think: I think my **data role** plan dies in 2028.
I'd have **three years** as an operator before robots arrive.
do: Turn the printing side into a **small business**.
S2.quote: AGI is the data guy, so my plan to be the data guy dies in 2028.
fieldNote: Yusuf's main plan is beaten by the **fast** picture.
He'd **hide** worry to keep younger colleagues calm.
He moves toward **owning** tools rather than doing tasks.

steps.text: Turn 3D printing into a custom parts business
Use AI to design and quote custom parts
Keep six months of rent untouched in savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read the card as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots 2034. Better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good warning, use it. With friends I'd say start learning now, don't wait. Online I'd share what I'm doing step by step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have time to be the process technician for a few years and then move to robot commissioning. By 2034 I'd be thirty-five, with skills nobody at the plant has today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the process technician job and the data course in year one. I'd keep the printing side, but as a hobby that pays. I'd start saving toward buying a small workshop unit in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly I feel ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a workshop unit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So I own something. If work changes, having a workshop with machines in it is better than having nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anyone you'd bring with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Aziz, he's twenty and on the packing line. I'd teach him the printers and get him on the course with me.

say: I'd call **five years** a good warning that people should actually use.
I'd share my **step by step** plan online.
think: I think I'd go from **process technician** to robot commissioning.

S3.quote: If work changes, having a workshop with machines in it is better than having nothing.
fieldNote: Yusuf wants to **own** a workshop as security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read the card as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty and people should stop worrying and start learning. At work I'd run a lunchtime session on AI tools. Online I'd post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be calm. I'd have time to build a proper business and still have the job. I'd be thirty-nine when robots arrive, and I'd want to be the one who owns the robots, not the one replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to process technician, then robot commissioning within five years. I'd buy the workshop unit around year four. And I'd teach Aziz and anyone else who wants to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited about the workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the workshop do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small batch parts for local firms, printed and machined, with a robot arm doing the boring bits. I'd run it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That some people will wait ten years and then be shocked. Lazlo is like that. Ten years for him is just ten years of not changing.

think: I think I'd have time to build a proper **business**.
I want to be the one who **owns** the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be squeezed from both sides, the thinking side and then the robots. What would help is cheap loans for small workshops, so operators like me can own machines instead of just running them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who owns the machines. That's what decides everything. A robot that I own is a good day, and a robot my boss owns is a bad one.

headlineQuote: A robot that I own is a good day, and a robot my boss owns is a bad one.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old** aluminium extrusion operator who uses AI daily.
He lives alone, has **five months** saved, and runs a small **3D printing** side business.
He sees most pictures as a **chance** to move into tuning and commissioning machines.
Only **AGI by 2028** makes him anxious, because it takes his data role plan away.
His answer to change is to **own** machines rather than be replaced by them.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be **squeezed** from both sides.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **loans** for small workshops so operators can **own machines**.
